title: Mahatma Gandhi's Talisman: The Face of the Poorest Man
culture_region: India / Greece / USA / South Africa / World

full_text:
In August 1947, as the joy of independence was clouded by the agony of partition riots, newly appointed cabinet ministers, planners, and civil servants approached Mahatma Gandhi in Delhi:
"Bapu, we are tasked with governing a free India. How can we ensure that our policies remain just and true? Give us a talisman to guide our decisions!"

Gandhi picked up a scrap of paper and penned a short paragraph that has become the moral compass of democratic governance worldwide:

"I will give you a talisman:
Whenever you are in doubt, or when the self becomes too much with you, apply the following test:

**Recall the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen, and ask yourself:
Is the step you contemplate going to be of any use to him?
Will he gain anything by it?
Will it restore to him control over his own life and destiny?
In other words, will it lead to Swaraj for the hungry and spiritually starving millions?**

Then you will find your doubts and your self melting away."

Gandhi's Talisman is not a religious mantra, but an infallible ethical test for every human being who wields power, wealth, or knowledge.

This is the crowning lesson of our one hundred great leaders' debates and dialogues:
True greatness is not measured by crowns, conquest, or eloquent vanity.
It is found in the courage to speak truth to power, to laugh in the face of adversity, and to dedicate one's life to the upliftment of the humblest among us!
moral: Every decision must be tested against its impact on the most vulnerable; compassionate service to humanity is the highest human virtue.
